target: AG1’s claim that AI is broadly beneficial because it improves convenience, health, accessibility, and workplace safety
objection: Those benefits do not come for free: automation can reduce job security and worker bargaining power, AI health tools can expose sensitive data to privacy and surveillance harms, assistive systems can fail in ways that seriously hurt disabled users, and AI safety systems can create false confidence by missing hazards or reducing human oversight.

target: AG1’s assumption that AI’s harms are manageable if used responsibly
objection: The promise of “responsible use” is often not enforceable in practice because AI can reproduce bias from training data, and governments or institutions may not be able to keep pace with deployment or verify that safeguards are actually being followed.

target: AG2’s portrayal of AI harms as unavoidable and inherent
objection: AG2 treats privacy, bias, and overreliance as if they are inevitable properties of AI rather than implementation problems; AG1 argues these risks can be reduced through design choices, governance, and responsible deployment.

target: AG2’s claim that AI necessarily harms jobs and the economy
objection: Automation does not have to mean net job loss; with retraining, wage supports, and incentives for productive uses, AI can reduce drudgery, increase productivity, and shift demand toward higher-skill work rather than simply eliminating jobs.

target: AG2’s claim that AI necessarily requires intrusive data collection and surveillance
objection: AI systems can be built with data minimization, consent, auditing, privacy-preserving techniques, and on-device processing, so the privacy risk is not inevitable.

target: AG2’s claim that AI cannot reliably support accessibility
objection: AI errors are not unique to AI, and accessibility tools can be made safer with testing, fallback options, human support, and user controls; when done well, AI expands independence for people with disabilities.

target: AG2’s claim that AI workplace safety is too unreliable to trust
objection: Safety systems can be explicitly designed to require human confirmation, use clear thresholds, log decisions, and monitor continuously, so AI can improve hazard detection and response time without eliminating human oversight.

target: AG2’s claim that AI undermines critical thinking and learning
objection: AI can also strengthen critical thinking if it coaches students step by step, asks Socratic questions, generates practice problems, and forces justification of answers; the effect depends on how it is integrated into learning.

target: AG2’s claim that AI inevitably reproduces and amplifies racial bias
objection: Bias can be measured across groups, mitigated with better data and modeling choices, and constrained by policy and procurement standards, so bias is not destiny.

target: AG1’s assumption that governance can reliably control AI harms at scale
objection: Oversight is often not realistically enforceable because training data, model internals, and evaluation methods are proprietary, deployment moves faster than regulators, and companies have incentives to ship first and fix later.

target: AG1’s claim that business incentives can be aligned with safety through guardrails
objection: Profit motives push companies toward more data collection and more automation, while safeguards like data minimization and human oversight add cost, so firms are likely to weaken them when they conflict with revenue.

target: AG1’s privacy-preserving AI proposal
objection: Even if some processing is on-device, AI systems still collect identifiers, usage logs, and behavioral signals, and consent is often not meaningful because users cannot negotiate terms or fully understand what is collected.

target: AG1’s claim that bias can be sufficiently controlled through audits and monitoring
objection: Bias is not simply a bug to be fixed; it can reappear under distribution shifts and feedback loops, so audits may reduce some harms but do not guarantee fairness.

target: AG1’s reliance on human-in-the-loop safety
objection: Human oversight can fail because people trust automation too much, leading to complacency or rubber-stamping; the problem is not just model accuracy but human overreliance on persuasive systems.

target: AG1’s belief that risk-based, enforceable AI governance is practical
objection: Risk classification itself is contestable and can be gamed, because firms may label systems as merely “assistive” or “narrow” even when they shape decisions at scale, undermining the whole gating framework.

target: AG1’s claim that rollback and monitoring can address AI harms after deployment
objection: Once a biased or privacy-invasive system has influenced hiring, credit, education, or other outcomes, the harm may already be done, so post hoc monitoring does not prevent the injury.

target: AG1’s assumption that continuous monitoring can coexist with privacy protection
objection: Monitoring usually requires collecting behavioral or telemetry data to detect drift and errors, which recreates the same privacy and surveillance harms the guardrails were supposed to avoid.

target: AG1’s reliance on liability and procurement standards to enforce accountability
objection: Victims still face high barriers because they must prove causation and obtain evidence from opaque systems, so legal accountability is slower and weaker than the pace of deployment.

target: AG1’s claim that detection, labeling, and takedown can manage AI-generated deception
objection: AI-enabled fraud, deepfakes, and misinformation scale too quickly; by the time misleading content is detected or removed, financial, reputational, and psychological damage may already have occurred.

target: AG1’s suggestion that AI misuse can be countered without broad restriction
objection: Countermeasures themselves can require large-scale content analysis or user tracking, which reintroduces privacy and surveillance risks and can also create chilling effects.

target: AG1’s reliance on provenance tools such as watermarks and signatures
objection: Watermarks and provenance markers can be removed, altered, or bypassed through editing, re-encoding, paraphrasing, or generation pipelines, so they are not reliable enough to stop deception at scale.

target: AG1’s claim that defensive AI offsets offensive AI
objection: Even if AI helps detect forgeries or support fact-checking, the overall effect is still more exposure to manipulation, so defensive uses do not cancel the harm created by offensive uses.

target: AG1’s claim that layered defenses can reduce deception without intrusive surveillance
objection: Content scanning, provenance verification, and takedown pipelines still depend on massive ingestion and logging, which functions as surveillance infrastructure even if it does not track explicit person-level profiles.

target: AG1’s claim that broad restriction would harm accessibility more than it helps
objection: Accessibility does not require general-purpose high-capability AI; narrower tools, human support, and non-generative assistive systems can meet many disability needs without the broader risks of AI.

target: AG1’s privacy-aware scanning proposal
objection: Even if retention is limited at runtime, detection systems are built and tuned on large amounts of user-like data, so the privacy risk is not eliminated but merely shifted to development and training phases.

target: AG1’s claim that graduated interventions such as warnings or demotion are neutral and fair
objection: Friction changes what people see and trust, and if the model is biased or calibrated on majority behavior, minority communities can face more false positives and informational suppression.

target: AG1’s view that risk-based gating can contain general-purpose AI
objection: General-purpose AI is quickly repurposed into borderline or high-impact uses, so the distinction between low-risk and high-risk applications becomes unstable and easy to evade.

target: AG1’s claim that privacy-preserving methods can make detectors safe enough to use
objection: Independent evaluation still depends on vendor-controlled access to data, logs, and traces, so the safeguard remains constrained by the same ecosystem that profits from deployment.

target: AG1’s proposal to license or gate high-risk capabilities
objection: Capabilities can be fine-tuned, distilled, and redistributed, making licensing enforcement an arms race that is hard to police once models are widely available.

target: AG1’s claim that AI can be used for learning without undermining critical thinking
objection: Even with scaffolding, people still learn to outsource writing, reasoning, and decisions to AI outputs, which gradually erodes judgment and independent skill.

target: AG1’s claim that deployment rules can solve economic and power-related harms
objection: AI development and deployment concentrate power among a few firms that control models, data pipelines, and distribution, increasing dependency and weakening workers’ and small businesses’ bargaining power.

target: AG1’s claim that restrictions on deployment can be kept clear and enforceable
objection: AI is bundled into ordinary products and productivity tools, so the line between low-stakes and high-stakes use becomes blurred and hard to enforce in practice.

target: AG1’s claim that vendor-provided disclosures and confidential audits create accountability
objection: When the key evidence and decision logic remain hidden from affected people, accountability exists only for regulators, not for the communities experiencing harm.

target: AG1’s belief that education and rules can prevent dependency on AI
objection: The convenience and productivity incentives of AI still encourage users to substitute AI for their own thinking, so rules cannot fully overcome the tendency toward dependence.
